subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO ESTABLISH STANDING JOINT PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the National Capital Commission is not sufficiently accountable to those who live in the national capital region or the people of Canada, and exercises its powers in an arbitrary manner without adequate consultation with other levels of government and that, as a just step, there should be a permanent standing joint committee on the national capital region.
She said: Mr. Speaker, sometimes it is said that it is the last straw that breaks the camel's back, and I am certain that the government is wondering at the rash of editorials over the weekend and at the press coverage of the appointment of the new chairman of the National Capital Commission, the former hon. member for Westmount. I think it is the straw that breaks the camel's back, because one of the things the people who live and work in this city and who pay taxes have felt is that the NCC has become a political football to this government and has not taken in the cares and concerns of those who live and work in this whole region.
It was Harold L. Ickes who said "I am against government by crony". Public office is a public trust, not a political prize. The recent appointments to the chairmanship of the National Capital Commission suggest that the job qualifications for that position have more to do with partisan public relations and assembly of land than the long range development of the national capital region. It seems that candidates for this position have to be former politicians who are closely linked with the present government.
The future of this city and important relations involving many levels of government across provincial jurisdictions need strong and enlightened leadership. The federal government, however, has completely ignored any but the most partisan considerations in the appointment of the NCC chairman. The ability of the former member for Westmount and of Mr. Juneau are not the issue. At a time when the NCC is at the centre of serious problems in this region, its whole operation must be an example of justice and accountability, both in fact and in appearance.
The NCC has now become what is really a national capital corporation in which the "capital" is represented in the dollars and cents of land management and powerplays redirect millions of dollars worth of buildings without the consultation of local elected people, and not in the creation of a meaningful symbol for our country.
The National Capital Act passed in 1958 states that the purpose of the NCC is to prepare plans and to assist in the development of the national capital region "in accordance with its national significance". Is there national significance in the fact that no elected official of any of the regional or local municipalities of the national capital region sits on the NCC?
January 30, 1978

In April of 1977 Mr. Pierre Juneau said:
-it is the duty of the NCC to nurture and expand the spirit of co-operation and good will which characterizes its relationship with the community of which it is an inseparable part.
But in its 1975-76 annual report, the NCC maintained that municipal responsibilities "cannot be construed as representing the national interest". It is tragic. How is this statement expected, again in the words of Mr. Juneau, to "expand the spirit of co-operation and good will"?
For most of its history the NCC and its predecessors concerned themselves with the beautification of the capital area. During the 1950s the commission began to assume the job of over-all planning. As the owner of upwards of 40 per cent of the land in the national capital region, the NCC has exerted a strong influence here and has been able to build whatever it wanted on its land without even getting a building permit.
Local groups and politicians have faced a deaf ear when they tried to become involved in their own planning and decision making in their city. There are many examples. The situation at Carlsbad Springs is just one of them, and it is a corner of my wonderful constituency of Ottawa-Carleton.
In 1974 farmers at Carlsbad Springs who wished to discuss expropriation plans involving their lands were told to report their complaints to a tape recorder since no authorized person was available to answer questions. It is no wonder that people at Carlsbad Springs were prompted to say:
We are just not happy with the NCC's behaviour. Poor communications with area residents was the standard pattern and often we would learn of events through press reports.
Mr. Juneau made a solemn commitment to me that he would meet with the residents of Carlsbad Springs, and now he is gone. There have been six chairmen in ten years, and five general managers. The heavy hand of this kind of bureaucratic decision breaks the spirit of people who live in that area. Sometimes I really wish that I could have taken Mr. Juneau up and made him listen to those wonderful farmers who love that land out there, who produce excellent market gardens, but who only live on year to year leases, men who really care about their land ant that it be productive, but yet have no sense of future from the commission.
The recent relocation of federal public servants to Hull is a failure as a planning effort. We have created some of the worst work ghettos. I do not say that certain public servants should not have gone. We should have evened out development on both sides, but producing those cement work ghettos to me is like planning out of a dark age. I have repeatedly received complaints from public servants, not because they had to move to Hull, but because they have to work in giant cold buildings with no souls. If that is the kind of planning which goes on in the Department of Public Works and in the National Capital Commission, we need some fresh air.
Local municipal officials in both Ottawa-Carleton and in the Outaouais region have been justifiably critical of the lack
National Capital Commission
of consultation and information which accompanied the relocation. For many residents of western Quebec the federal relocation to Hull is better described as interference. There is a sense that federal buildings such as Place du Portage are destroying the French culture and language by destroying existing neighbourhoods. I have a feeling we could have done much better.
While all of that was going on, no one thought through the planning process of what should take place here in this city. There were no plans regarding Rideau Centre: it was all talk. There is an incredible number of empty parking spots two blocks away from this beautiful building. There was no planning whatsoever.
The Auditor General has criticized the NCC for a financial arrangement it made with the Department of Public Works involving $22 million for the purchase of land in the central core of Ottawa. Rather than follow the directions of the orders in council authorizing the purchase of these properties, the NCC made an arrangement which avoided the need to seek parliamentary authority for such moves. Planning by the NCC has often been marked, not by the spirit of co-operation about which Mr. Juneau spoke, but by an inclination to move unilaterally. The regional and provicial governments have been moved to call for a reduction of NCC powers in a number of areas. They have called for a reduction of NCC power to expropriate land, for an end to federal intervention in the planning field, and for a realignment of NCC powers to make them more narrow.
It has been suggested that the NCC remove itself from planning altogether and merely be responsible for such things as cultural development in the national capital region. The NCC plan for the national capital region, called "Tomorrow's Capital", favours centralized growth in one area, but the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton plan favours decentralization to a number of areas. Such sharp differences between non-elected officials and elected bodies from the provinces suggest the adoption of a requirement that NCC plans agree with local and regional plans before they become official.
Under the BNA Act the provinces are responsible for municipal affairs, including planning. This planning is often delegated to regional and local officials, yet the federal government, through the NCC, seems to believe that it is the only one which has the constitutional power to plan for the development of the "national interest" in this region. What we need is a definition of what is the national interest. The lack of a proper forum for discussion of the national interest has contributed to intergovernmental tensions.
The legal mandate of the NCC to develop the national capital has become instead a mandate for secret decisions. Rather than sensing the mood of Ottawa and Hull in a spirit of open government, the NCC has operated as a remote, self-sustaining wing of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) office. Sometimes public servants and residents of the city of Ottawa say they have canals and bike paths. We remember the famous time in history when it was said: "Let's give them

January 30, 1978
National Capital Commission
bread and circuses". That was to divert attention from the fact that in this town we pay higher taxes and a commercial industrial rate about 20 per cent higher than in any other area of Ontario. This is due to the fact that the federal government does not pay its share.
In 1972 journalist Patrick Watson, writing in Maclean's, described the "Cool Trippers" who exist in many government offices. Cool trippers survive and keep the great machine going, not by correcting problems, but by being consummate experts in tolerating the intolerable. Problems are not solved; solutions are not found. Long-term development has given way to maintenance of the status quo through an agency which lacks accountability, access, and openness.
Prior to Christmas there was a breath of hope that this committee would be formed and that we would be well on our way, but half the time of the committee has now gone by and we have not even decided who should be on this committee. That is the kind of thing which makes people feel that the matter of the future of the region has been shoved to one side.
At present it is unclear just what type of consultation takes place. We need a formal, consultative and co-ordinating mechanism to ensure that planning in the national capital region is thorough and based on dialogue, not arbitrary and hidden directives. That is why 1 believe that the federal government might well consider its commitment to consultation and accountability through a standing committee on the national capital region with representatives from all levels of government. I believe it is here in this parliament that there should be input with regard to the public interest and to the future of the national capital region.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO ESTABLISH STANDING JOINT PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that 1 support this motion. 1 commend the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) for introducing it to this House. I cannot agree with all the remarks she has made in the course of this debate, but I am in substantial agreement with the general thrust of her complaint about the National Capital Commission.
Contrary to the opinion of the hon. lady who just spoke, I believe that the new chairman of the National Capital Commission will make a great contribution in that position. He brings to it a very great background of experience. He is sensitive, he is a bilingual person, and he knows as much as any member of this House or anyone outside it the problems of this region and the special character of the national capital. At this stage of his career it is a challenge for him to prove that he can make this further contribution and leave his mark. I believe he is so motivated, and I look forward to a good chairmanship and a good regime under the former member for Westmount.
That is not to say that I am not without reservations about what is going on. I cannot help but express my concern about the fact that a motion adopted on December 13 in this House to strike a joint committee of this place and the other place to deal with matters of the National Capital Commission has not been followed through. It is now 48 days since the motion was

passed, and the committee was given instructions to bring its report in within 90 days. This is manifestly impossible. The time will have to be extended, and there is very important work to be done.
There are many things one could say about the National Capital Commission. The very concept of running a national capital through a Crown corporation is something which has always puzzled me. The National Capital Commission is not elected, as the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton said. There is not a single elected person on the commission. The commission talks about its mandate. I have attended public meetings at which planners for the commission talked about their mandate, as if nobody else in the room had a mandate and as if elected people had no mandate at all.
According to those planners, only this Crown corporation, the existence of which is at the decree of the executive, has a mandate to do great things. It is my hope that members of this temporary joint committee-the motion before us would create a permanent one-would go to Washington for a short visit. We can learn a great deal from Washington's experience. There is a body in Washington called the National Capital Planning Commission. That body is not permitted to have title to one acre of land. That body is restricted to an advisory and planning capacity, and that came out of the bitter experience of what happened in Washington when an authoritative federal agency tried to deal with a heavy hand and misused ownership of land in an attempt to impose its view.
No clearer example of misuse of the power of land ownership can be seen than in the present National Capital Commission. Members of the NCC and spokesmen for them appeared before the joint committee over a year ago and argued that they had a vision as to how the national capital should be planned. There was a day when they alone had the technical expertise to do planning, but the growth of planning capacity in the regional municipality on the Quebec side, Communaute Regionale de l'Outaouais, and in the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton on this side has brought an entirely new element into the picture. The planning resources at local disposal are substantially in excess of the planning resources at the disposal of the National Capital Commission.
When the National Capital Commission publishes a document, such as "Invitation to Dialogue", which it published in 1975, it said it would create a community of 100,000 in Carlsbad and 100,000 on the other side of the river near Aylmer, and link them with a transportation corridor, a corridor going from a place where no one existed to another place where no one existed, at a time when we have negative growth forecast in the national capital region itself and the government is implementing a policy of decentralization. The National Capital Commission have given the figure of 25,000 jobs-that is their figure-to be moved out of the national capital region as part of the decentralization process. They mentioned that figure in their 1975 annual report. I am happy to note that that figure has been substantially revised down-
January 30, 1978

wards in the order of 15,000 jobs, of which only 5,000 are permanent.
Nevertheless it was inconceivable to me what monstrously bad planning advice the NCC offered. Then it said to the regional municipalities: "If you don't conform to our vision of how things are going to be, you can't cross our land". They own large blocks of land in this region, and they threatened in an arbitrary, tryannical, irresponsible fashion to thwart the plans of the regional municipalities, plans which were arrived at after extensive public hearings in a democratic way, because they did not conform to the ideals of those heaven-sent planners hired by the Crown corporation called the National Capital Commission.
If we can learn anything from the Washington experience it is that we cannot create a body with excessive powers which are essentially based on land ownership. And based on its current concept of its mandate it should not be permitted, although theoretically responsible to an elected body, indirectly to the cabinet through its Crown corporation status, to act in the way that the Auditor General criticized when they subverted the will of parliament in the exchange of properties they had no business acquiring, in the way in which they kept their books, and in the way they let contracts without tenders.
There is a house cleaning job to be done in that commission. I want to say, to the credit of the former chairman, who I think was a conscientious and good chairman, that he became aware of the magnitude of the problem and he kept a low profile. He quietly worked at improving relations and brought a personal integrity to his job, and I want to pay tribute to him for that on this occasion.
The task of re-examining the powers and functions of the National Capital Commission is an imperative task. Those of us who are residents of the area say to the members of this place and the other place who will serve on that committee: "Please take an interest and do a job." We want this capital to be a place that is a showpiece, a pride, a symbol of Canadian nationhood. We want it to be a place where the two official languages and the various cultures that have made this country will all feel at home; a place where there is a part of them in this national symbol. But we want it also to be a democratic capital with its two systems of property and civil law, one on the Quebec side and one on the Ontario side; a capital with its two systems of education, and the multiplicity that is involved in the most complicated national capital that any nation in the modern world has attempted to create. The task, Mr. Speaker, is a very great task. I hope that the committee will be struck and that the terms of reference will be before it shortly. I hope too that hon. members will proceed and a report will follow which will be of great assistance to the government and the new chairman for setting the policy for the years ahead.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO ESTABLISH STANDING JOINT PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even though the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) may have some matters on which they do not agree, they are in agreement on what is being asked for, both in this motion and in the motion in the name of the hon. member for Ottawa
National Capital Commission
West, although that one is not before us today. In both cases they are seeking some democratization of the operations of the National Capital Commission. That is a position, Mr. Speaker, that I think should be fully supported by this House.
I was glad to hear the hon. member for Ottawa West say a few things which make it clear that he realizes, even though he is an Ottawa resident, that there is a sense in which this area belongs to Canada. It is the nation's capital. It is appropriate that the people of Canada through their parliament and their government should have something to say about what goes on in the planning of this general area. As I say, no one quarrels with that. But from that position the National Capital Commission seems to have evolved in a way which, as both previous speakers have pointed out, includes no elected members and operates on its own self-created mandate. I believe that point has been made today by the two members from Ottawa who have already spoken and who deserve our full support. I hope they will stick with it, and that other members from the Ottawa area as well as some of us who have spent quite a few years in the Ottawa area will also continue to do so.
Having said that, I have no desire to prevent others from speaking or to contribute to the talking out of this motion; I would like to see it carried. I realize there is a problem of whether we want a special committee or a standing committee, that some negotiations may have to take place, but I hope the opinion of the House this afternoon will be clearly in favour, as I say, of the democratization of the running of the National Capital Commission.
While I am on my feet, may I say that I know there is hardly anybody in the House who does not know what is on my mind, but I want to say again that I greatly deplore the lack of planning that has resulted in this cluster of high rise structures in one part of this city. I have often spoken about this from the point of view of one who lives a few miles away and can still see the Peace Tower from my bedroom window out on Com-manche Drive. Woe betide the developer who happens to put a highrise building between me and the Peace Tower!
I have spoken about this from the viewpoint of those who are on the ground. There are areas in many parts of the city where one used to be able to see the Peace Tower when driving around, but now in most areas it is blocked out. A couple of times lately when flying in and out of the city I have had a particularly good view of the place. Usually my flights in and out of the city are over Parkwood Hills and Kanata and on we go; we come in on that same runway time and time again. But a couple of times lately on clear days the plane has circled around to the east and we have been able to see the whole of the city at once. It hits me between the eyes when I look down and see those clusters of highrise buildings all in one place. They should at least have been spread out. Some are in the suburbs but most are right in the centre of the city, and unfortunately, it is creating a core which is an eyesore and which does not make any sense. Indeed, from the air one can hardly see the Peace Tower, because of all the other high structures. I think it is contrary to the whole idea expressed by the hon. member for Ottawa West that this is the nation's

January 30, 1978
National Capital Commission
capital. This being the nation's capital, I think this building and its Peace Tower have a symbolism which is very important, and I am sorry that that symbolism and that view have to a large extent been blotted out. You cannot ask anyone to tear down these tall buildings, but I hope there will be some better planning of this city in the years that lie ahead.
Towards that end, I support the whole idea that the planning of this area should be done in a democratic way. Therefore, I commend the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton for the motion she has brought before the House this afternoon.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO ESTABLISH STANDING JOINT PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take part in this debate on motion No. 17 presented by the member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott). It does seem that this motion is excellent but it is twofold. The first part is a critic addressed to the National Capital Commission and concerns its actions since its inception. That is the negative part of it. The other part is rather constructive. It states that a permanent joint committee should be constituted.
First of all, let me say that I do not favour the creation of a permanent joint committee but rather that of a permanent committee of the House of Commons which, when parliament is in session, would study the complaints and concerns of the various groups and municipalities in the national capital region. I think there is something like it in Washington which is called the District of Columbia committee made out of representatives from the Congress who, every year, study the problems facing the District of Columbia, be it concerning estimates or other matters. In my opinion this is an excellent idea.
What we should recall is that we must always take into account the history of the National Capital Commission and the national capital region itself. I have heard the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) criticize the skyline which is now hiding the magnificent view of parliament but it all boils down to say that if we had listened to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, we would have today some kind of a federal district and this would never have happened.
If we have high-rise buildings hiding Parliament Hill from just about everywhere-and the same kind of planning, the same type of design took place on the Quebec side-it is precisely because there have been quarrels among politicians while the National Capital Commission or the Federal District Commission as it was called then, opposed the construction of these high-rise buildings. However, the Federal District Commission had no jurisdiction over the Ottawa city council nor dit it have any such authority over the municipalities in the national capital region. And if we study the act which governs the National Capital Commission, we realize that it is not vested with any power.
If we now have problems with the National Capital Commission, it is because, like my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) has already said, there have been many changes and extraordinary evolution in the national

capital area. Before there were no regional communities on either side of the river. There were simply municipalities which could not afford urban planners. In fact, urban planners were rare at that time and municipal authorities used to borrow the services of National Capital Commission urban planners to develop rural municipalities and cities within the national capital area.
But this has changed. Nowadays nearly all cities hire urban planners. They have consultants. Urban planners are like economists: Half will say that such and such a project is good for a certain area and the other half will say that it is unpractical. It is somewhat like writers who can write very good novels but whose stories would seem ridiculous if they were applied to reality. They are nice stories, but they could not happen in practice. It is the people who have spoiled the structures of the National Capital Commission, and it did have weaknesses in the past. In my opinion, it no longer has.
It has had certain inherent human weaknesses because its destiny is controlled by human beings and its mandate comes from the government. I hear the opposition critics say: Oh, those are political appointments. Whether it be the Liberal or the Progressive Conservative government, I am sure that the Conservative government made certain appointments around 1958; I am not sure, but I have the impression that it did. But in the present case, the case of Mr. Drury, who has been appointed chairman of the commission, I am sure he will do an excellent job. When he takes over his office, I am sure that his first request will not be for a map of the region to see where he is, and this, at least, is something. He has been living in the area for 30 years. He served as Minister of Public Works, and we know what the NCC owes him during that term, since at the time the Commission came under Public Works.
So we had several chairmen, and since then evolution followed its normal course. We did not use to hear about the NCC. In the Ottawa-Hull area, people used to phone their members of parliament to ask when the NCC would be expropriating them, and that was going on on both sides. Everybody was waiting to be expropriated. There were not that many expropriations, but let us say that everybody waited for the NCC before selling their house and property which often were not worth anything. And I think that the NCC has changed. At that time, we did not use to hear about it because, as I said earlier, the professional services of the NCC were used on both sides, so we did not use to hear about it, and it was a good thing at the time. But today this has degenerated into conflicts of interest between experts, and I think that experts are not worth anything. They are good once in a while when a war breaks out in order to know whether the cannon is going to fire left or right, because a cannon that fires to the left when it is aimed at right is no good. That is all right. And, besides, they are ideologists, people who try to put down on paper things that do not make sense.

And then Mr. Juneau "arrived" while the National Capital Commission was going through an adjustment process with all the changes that had occurred in the region. At first Mr. Juneau was not accepted by representatives of different municipal bodies from either side but in the end everybody deplored his departure. But everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as someone leaves, he is offered congratulations and all sorts of good things, even from his opponents. But he had gained the confidence of the public.
Now we have a new chairman and I am sure he will render exceptional services to the population and more particularly to the national capital region. He will do so because the leaders of this region should understand that if we are part of the national capital region, we should depoliticize our problems. I believe we should try a formula to reflect in the national capital area the best of Canada's beauty and greatness. It must be the nation's focus and soul. Certainly this cannot be done amidst dissension or it cannot be built on bickering, or great walls of China. It can only be done in a spirit of co-operation.
Mr. Speaker, speaking of co-operation the thing that struck me most in Washington were the various frameworks ruling the District of Columbia. But before discussing that I must say it would be a great thing if all members of the National Capital commission were elected. Unfortunately there can be no agreement at the municipal government level, nor at the regional community level, so how can there be agreement when they are part of two different entities? Each time provincial governments come here, people from the area catch cold or pneumonia, and the impact is on the NCC. Every time Toronto says to do something Ottawa complies, and every time Quebec says something, Hull follows. How then can there be co-operation? This is a total mess!
If on the other hand we had elected people, people representing Canada as a whole, because in this way is the National Capital Commission formed, if we had a chairman nominated not on account of political allegiance, not because the government is Liberal, but chosen among senators, judges, Progressive Conservatives because of his qualifications, as was done in the past without any outcry.
So let me come back to my experience in the District of Columbia. It might be a good thing if elective representatives in the area pressed reeves to group themselves into in a council of governments as was done in the District of Columbia. This
National Capital Commission
is an assembly comprised of representatives of all groups within the District of Columbia. Those elective representatives meet in general assembly to elect a ten-man executive. Members of that executive group neither govern nor control, because they have no power other than persuasion. Whenever there are differences among governments on a given project, those members go back and forth between governments to convince them it is in the region's greater interest. It is something in the nature of a guiding light or a life buoy.
In my view, the various municipal councils in the area should meet along those lines, they should create an executive to do some lobbying with the various levels of government, for the good administration of the national capital area. For example, we have the convention centre. The battle is on. Will Hull have it, will Ottawa have it, who knows? Everybody is lobbying. It should not be that way. If economic development is what we want for this region, we should decide and say: this time you will have it, next time it will be our turn, all in order to spur the economy and create economic benefits for the entire region.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, we should not let this become a political sounding board, and I think the National Capital Commission has played a vital role in that matter. Of course, the committee will make recommendations, and I am sure that in view of the developments of the last 15 years, the government will not lend a deaf ear, and will do what it has to do to keep in step and give the national capital the best of all possible governments. I am not sure that if we had gone along with the idea of a federal district we would not know all the problems we find ourselves enmeshed in today. Regardless of political allegiances, we should all work in the same direction, in order to create an image, a crystallisation of all the aspirations described by politicians and prime ministers on the topic of a capital of a country, a nation, Ottawa. That is why I think we failed for not doing it, and that is why we find ourselves a bit short-handed today, trying to patch up that which was excellent in the beginning, but which was unfortunately left to stagnate for the past 50 years.
Mr. Speaker, those are the few comments I wanted to make on this motion, and as I said at the outset, this is a two part motion, one being critical, negative and political, the other being constructive, except that I would not want to see the Senate sit on this committee, but rather a committee of the House which would review the funds, complaints, and studies, and which would hear the citizens at least once a year.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT BASIC RATE OF WAR DISABILITY PENSION BE RECONSIDERED
VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT BASIC RATE OF WAR DISABILITY PENSION BE RECONSIDERED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, January 25, as recorded in Hansard at page 2232, I put this question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald):
In view of the increasing concern on the part of veterans across Canada over the refusal of the government to restore the basic rate of the war disability pension to the average take-home pay of the five categories of public servants designated in 1973, has the minister resubmitted this matter to the cabinet, asking for a reversal of the negative decision which he announced a couple of months ago?
The reply of the Minister of Veterans Affairs was in these words:
No, Mr. Speaker, I have not resubmitted this question, but I would like to remind the House that on January 1 there was an increase of 7.2 per cent in disability pensions across this country. As I stated previously, when the government sees things in a different light, I will bring this matter back to it.
January 30, 1978

In my supplementary question I pointed out that the 7.2 per cent increase which came into effect this month because of legislation that is on the statute books was something entirely different from the restoration of the basic rate to the formula agreed upon in 1973. It was this that I asked the minister to take back again to cabinet.
In my supplementary I also referred to the problem which still exists in that when a veteran dies having been on a pension of less than 48 per cent there is no automatic pension for his widow. I also pointed out that there is still no compensation available to veterans who were prisoners of war in the first world war. I underline the urgency of these two matters which I brought forward in my supplementary but tonight I shall speak mainly on the question of the basic rate.
I might say that the Minister of Veterans Affairs has expressed to me his regret that he could not be here tonight to give his personal reply to the question I am raising, and I assume the parliamentary secretary will be making the reply. I want to say to the parliamentary secretary that seldom will he be called upon to deal with a more important issue of principle than the one involved in this question. It is not just the standard request for more money.
There is a lot of history behind this. Before I was elected to this chamber, in fact shortly after the first world war, disability pensions were set up on the basis of 100 per cent disability being related to a certain level of pay in the civil service, as it was then called. But over the decades this standard got worn down so that by the time of the second world war the principle had been lost and disability pensions under the Pension Act were set arbitrarily. During the second world war we tried to get back to an acceptable formula and we kept trying in the years which followed. Finally, in 1973, after a tripartite committee and the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs had studied the question and made recommendations, the government agreed to set the 100 per cent disability rate at the level of the average take-home pay of five designated categories within the public service.
There was also the recommendation that this practice should be continued in perpetuity. The government did not accept this latter point of view but undertook to deal with that question later. It said: For the time being we will accept these figures for 1973 and increase pensions in succeeding years by the percentage by which the cost of living increases. That is what has happened since. The result is that a very wide gap has developed between the average pay of the federal public service in the five categories chosen and the amount of the 100 per cent disability pension.
What veterans are asking is good faith on the part of the government. They are asking that the principle fought for at the end of World War I and again at the end of World War II and finally won in 1973 be sustained. I plead with the parliamentary secretary not to say that the 7.2 per cent cost of living increase fills the bill. It does not. Veterans know what that does. It still leaves them behind the standard of living which
Adjournment Debate
can be attained by those who are able to work because they have not suffered war disability.
This is not just one more request by members of the opposition for more money to be spent here or there. We are asking for recognition of a principle which was sacred at the end of World War I, agreed upon at the end of World War II, and confirmed in 1973, a principle which is now being lost by the refusal of the government to restore the pension to the figure set by the 1973 formula.
My plea to the minister the other day was that he should take this matter back to cabinet despite the fact that he announced a few months ago that the answer was no. I hope the parliamentary secretary is in a position to assure us tonight that his minister recognizes the seriousness of this issue and that he will take the matter back to cabinet and seek a reversal of that negative decision during the present session of parliament.

As the hon. member knows, this question has been brought up repeatedly in this House. I am going to reiterate what has already been said about the 7.2 per cent increase which came about on January 1. However, one thing that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) did not mention was that the basic rate for an unmarried 100 per cent pensioner is now $596.70 per month. In the case of a married 100 per cent pensioner, the figure is $745.88 per month; and if he and his wife have two dependent children, his pension has been increased to $880.15 per month.
In so far as the pro rata pension to widows of pensioned veterans is concerned, there is nothing new to add since a statement was last made on this subject.
The suggestion has been made that a widow should receive a pro rata pension if her husband had been in receipt of a disability pension of 47 per cent or less. This is because she would be fully pensionable as a widow if his pension had been 48 per cent or more at the time of death. What is sometimes missed is that the widow will be pensioned if her husband's death occurred during wartime or was attributable to his service, regardless of the degree of the assessment of his disability.
The question which arises is whether, if death was not in any way attributable to military service, a widow's pension should be paid because of the service connection. We know and the hon. member knows-I say this in all sincerity-that the benefits provided to the disabled serviceman or woman, or to their surviving dependents, are far greater than those provided by most other countries. I am not aware of any of our major

With regard to providing pensions for first world war prisoners of war, the minister has stated and I repeat tonight, that this is under very active consideration and that a decision will be made shortly.
I have served with the hon. member for a number of years on the Standing Committee of Veterans Affairs. I would ask him if he would take those things which have been done into consideration. We hope that those things yet to be accomplished will come about very quickly.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGATION DEPARTMENT CIRCUMVENTING GROWTH GUIDELINES
PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGATION DEPARTMENT CIRCUMVENTING GROWTH GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I am calling for the subject of contracting out in the civil service and the hiring through private employment agencies to be referred to a standing committee. I also ask that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) be asked to appear before that committee to explain government policy in regard to these hiring practices which completely contradict his statement of February 16, 1977, that public service growth would be restricted to 0.6 per cent.
Growth is growth and this method of hiring through the backdoor requires an explanation from the government. The Public Service Alliance has launched an all-out campaign against these two practices and it is quite obvious that there is a complete breakdown in communication and consultation between the government and the alliance. It has almost reached the stage of open warfare.
To add to the complete confusion, private employment agencies claim there is a threat to their future. The minister should not only explain to the committee why all this extra growth is needed but why the government is not using the services of Canada Manpower when extra help is needed, especially when there are one million unemployed Canadians.
I should like to read into the record some of the concerns of the Public Service Alliance which are expressed in their publication, the Argus Journal. It is no wonder we have no morale in the public service. The alliance should also be allowed to appear before the committee to present its side of the story.
In one of the latest publications the alliance has printed a questionnaire for distribution to the membership. It is entitled "The Great Government Cover-up". The alliance urges its members to answer the questionnaire as fully as possible.
The concern is shown in another article headed "Contracting out: the Great Government Cover-Up", which states in part:
Contracting out is expensive: the government claims it is keeping down annual increases in the size of the public service while at the same time expanding work done for the government by private firms.
There is little or no control over the quality of or accountability for work done by private contractors.

Contracting out leaves politicians open to the temptation to give contracts to "friends" who might be supporters in past or future election campaigns.
There is even danger that some sections of government departments might disappear because of the increasing trend to contracting out.
Some firms that hold government contracts exploit their employees.
Another article states under the heading "Members' jobs are on the line as contracting out increases":
The loss of government jobs is a crucial issue but there is more to it than that. The PSAC has opposed contracting out for more reasons than job security.
First, it is dishonest. The government says it is limiting the growth of the public service; in fact it is using contracting out to cover up an expansion of service growth. While limiting public service spending, the government is increasing costly professional and special contractual services.
Another article is headed "New guidelines no solution" and states in part:
The government has drawn up new guidelines on the use by departments of temporary help in the administrative support category in the National Capital Region. But PSAC President Andy Stewart points out that the guidelines don't go far enough to eliminate the profit being raked off by middlemen. In Ottawa-Hull alone, he estimates, there are now more than 2,000 people in government offices who are supplied by personnel agencies.
The article goes on to state:
However, Brother Stewart says the only acceptable solution would be to do away entirely with temporary help employees.
"As an alternative, the Public Services Commission should establish a pool of qualified public service employees to draw on for temporary help. In this way the total payment for services would accrue to the employees themselves."
These alternatives should be fully discussed by a parliamentary committee.
I would also like to refer to a letter to the editor of the Winnipeg Tribune written by a MOT safety inspector. He states in part:
My colleagues and I service, maintain and certify all the complex communications, navigational aids, radar and electronics control equipment... To attempt to contract out to inexperienced, untrained, incapable maintenance personnel, the absolute requirement of high quality and availability of electronic services to everyone who flies in Canadian air space is a flagrant disregard for the SAFETY of anyone who flies.
To falsely claim to be saving the taxpayer money while at the same time heedlessly compromising your SAFETY and mine represents at the very least, a conscious criminal act.
In light of these serious charges and this continuing battle between the government and the civil service, I am sure the parliamentary secretary will say there is no alternative but to bring this whole subject matter out in the open by having it fully discussed before a parliamentary committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas H. Lefebvre (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGATION DEPARTMENT CIRCUMVENTING GROWTH GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is recognized that the use of temporary help company employees has been increasing over the last few years. Consequently the Treasury Board has recently approved and issued a policy statement and guidelines on the appropriate use of such services in the administrative support category in the national capital region. Under the guidelines, agency employees are to be used only where an unexpected vacancy or workload increase occurs without sufficient notice to carry out normal staffing action. Arrangements for temporary help will be limited to eight weeks' duration. In order to provide a measure
January 30, 1978

of control over the qualifications of personnel supplied through the agencies, and over rates paid, DSS will become the sole contracting authority for such services on April 1 of this year.
In order to provide a measure of control, the Department of Supply and Services will be the only government department with authority in these matters. In addition, departments are also being asked to maintain adequate records on the utilization of such services and to ensure that personnel provided meet the qualification standards specified in the contracts. At the end of one year these operations under the new system will be evaluated by the Treasury Board secretariat. It will evaluate the effectiveness of this policy and guidelines by utilizing departmental records and data supplied by the Department of Supply and Services. Changes have been made, and further attempts are being made to control this.
Further, it will be ensured that where possible public servants are replaced by other public servants through such actions as redeployment of existing resources, and use of transfers, acting appointments or specified period appointments, as appropriate, in accordance with the provisions of the Public Service Employment Act. Where there is temporary administrative work to be done for which no man-year or salary provisions were made, as far as possible such work will be done by existing departmental or program resources through the rearrangement of priorities and temporary reassignment of tasks to personnel. Where it is not feasible, temporary help company employees may be engaged. However, to avoid any duplication or any potential conflict with the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the Public Service Employment Act appointment criteria, they should not be engaged for periods in excess of eight weeks.
The Department of Supply and Services will become the sole contracting authority for temporary help services in the administrative support category as of April 1, 1978. Commencing April 1, 1978, departments and agencies will be asked to obtain temporary help services directly from those companies with which the Department of Supply and Services has entered standing offer agreements.
There is no doubt that the government shares the concern of the hon. member. Attempts are being made to make arrangements so that the best and most efficient use can be made of the public service in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is becoming very apparent that the government's food policy has become the joke of the agricultural industry. At the present time everyone is skeptical of three ministers: the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner).
Adjournment Debate
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has been the most conspicuous to date in putting his foot in his mouth. It appears that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs wants a cheap food policy. Last week during a press conference in Winnipeg he said that he was looking at a possible ceiling on food prices, reduction of import duties and other controls on domestic prices, export embargoes, selective consumer subsidies, possible two-price systems to set different prices for domestic and export consumption, stiffer supervision of food processors and distributors, a study of some of their most basic activities and their information system, and he would attempt to explain food price changes to consumers. That statement is enough to send everyone running for cover.
Amid all the speeches and meetings, what is really happening? Do we really need a national food policy when the proportion of personal incomes spent on food is probably the lowest in the world; when domestic production of many food items is at a permanent cost disadvantage; when domestic production of some important commodities is already declining; and when massive imports are worsening the balance of payments problems, which is a major threat to the national economy?
Obviously the answer must be no, we do not require a national food policy. In 1976 Canadians spent an average of 13.6 per cent of their disposable incomes on food eaten at home, compared to 14.8 per cent in 1971 and 19.5 per cent between 1951 and 1955. I believe that a food policy put forward by Trudeau Liberals means a cheap food policy.
The farmers will once again be caught in a government controlled vice with bureaucrats and government planners trying to squeeze every last cent out of the producer. A cheap food policy, if allowed to develop in the manner talked about by the minister's colleagues, would, in my opinion, virtually destroy the horticultural industry in Canada as well as major sectors of the beef and pork industries.
This program, the propaganda associated with it and also the February conference, are all being brought forward as political gimmicks designed for the 1978 election. The government is trying to please everyone, and of course that is impossible. To consumers it appears that a positive move is being made toward a food policy; but the unsuspecting producer will be made to feel that his interests are being looked after. Both these observations are incorrect. The government has no policy on anything except to re-elect itself. It will destroy and divide to do just that, and apparently that is what is coming out of the national food policy.
By agreeing to a national food policy, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has directed Canadian farmers to an uncertain and unknown future. I believe that we have a minister who is forced to go along with his cabinet colleagues, partly to save face because there is no coherent agricultural policy in this country, and partly from political expediency because the government anticipates an election, possibly this

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Caron (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to answer and supplement a reply given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on January 27, 1978 to a question by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta).
Perhaps the hon. member is not aware of the purpose of the Food Strategy Conference. It is not to dictate a food policy but to improve the procedures of communication, consultation and understanding for those who have a vital interest in the agricultural food system, either as consumers, producers, manufacturers, retailers or restaurateurs as well as dealers in the agriculture and food area.
We also want their opinions and recommendations for the implementation, the improvement as well as the continuity of a Canadian food strategy.
The government will spell out everything that has been accomplished and the directions we have already taken for a Canadian food strategy but I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that we did not decide to call this conference to dictate government ideas
but to exchange and receive the opinions of producers, consumers and people in the agricultural food industry in general.
The proposed consultations we undertook were aimed at a food strategy reached in three steps: the meetings between a committee of federal ministers and nine national organizations last December, the federal-provincial conference held in Winnipeg on January 16 and now the National Food Strategy Conference to be held on February 22 and 23, 1978. That conference will have the participation of over 150 organizations, and if I may be more specific, has already generated a lot of enthusiasm and support from various agricultural food organizations.
The food strategy is an aggressive concept to help improve the food policy now in effect in Canada.
The food system is important and complex and has very large significance for the economic life in this country. We are aggressively seeking as a department the assistance and active support of all Canadians with an interest in the food business.
